paper_title: AeroRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement for Aerial Vision-Language Navigation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to follow natural-language instructions, yet still fail frequently in closed-loop flight. Correcting these failures requires repairs, i.e., actions that avoid them at the states the policy itself reaches, which human pilots cannot label at scale and rule-based planners cannot supply reliably. In this paper, we present AeroRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework in which an aerial navigation policy iteratively learns from its own failures. Our key insight is that a failing policy should judge its own repairs by flying on from them. Judged in this way, its sampled actions and even rule-based proposals that hurt it when imitated directly become reliable supervision. Moreover, an episode terminates at its first failure, concealing subsequent failures until the earlier ones are repaired. AeroRSI thus renews its supervision in every round, anchoring the failures of the current policy, verifying repairs by its continuation, and distilling them while keeping its behavior elsewhere. On TravelUAV, three rounds raise the success rate of a supervised 2B-parameter policy from 46.4% to 67.5% and reduce collisions by half, surpassing the previous state of the art by 10.6 points from the same initialization without extra human labels or inference cost. Code and models are available at https://github.com/starsholic/AeroRSI.

sections.content: 1. Introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to follow natural-language instructions, yet still fail frequently in closed-loop flight. Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) that follow naturallanguage instructions could inspect infrastructure, search for people, and deliver goods without human pilot. Toward this goal, recent vision-language-action (VLA) models for aerial vision-language navigation (VLN) [27] directly map visual observations and instructions to flight actions [1, 811], mirroring their success in robotic manipulation [1216]. Despite this progress, existing aerial agents [1, 8, 9, 17, 18] still fail frequently in closed-loop flight, often due to collisions with obstacles. Since single wrong action can terminate an entire flight, such failures severely limit their reliability. These failures stem from well-known mismatch in imitation learning [1921], as policy trained on demonstrations reaches states that the demonstrations never cover and accumulates errors along the flight. Correcting them requires repairs, namely actions that avoid failure at the states the policy itself reaches, and existing approaches differ mainly in who judges such an action. Interactive imitation learning [2124] queries an expert for corrective actions, but human annotation is extremely expensive at scale, and rule-based planners [25, 26] ignore the language instruction. Automatic correction methods [1, 27, 28] avoid human labeling by deriving corrections from collision rollbacks, reference paths, or auxiliary teacher policies, yet they do not consider whether the policy can actually ex1 ecute these corrections. Reinforcement learning [18, 29 31] instead relies on episode-level rewards, which indicate whether flight fails but not which action should have been taken. As result, annotation-free, action-level supervision that the policy itself can execute remains missing. Recursive self-improvement offers promising route toward such supervision. It has recently achieved remarkable success in language models [3237], where model learns from its own verified outputs, and has begun to extend to robotics and navigation [28, 3843]. However, closed-loop flight poses three challenges that answer-level self-improvement leaves open. First, an answer can be verified on its own, whereas the value of flight action depends on the subsequent flight of the policy, which calls for step-level values as in process supervision [44, 45]. Second, language model learns from fixed set of problems, whereas flight terminates at its first failure, so later failures remain hidden until earlier ones are repaired. Third, self-improvement in language models mainly reinforces answers that the model can already produce [46, 47], whereas failing flight policy often cannot sample the action it needs, even though simple physical priors, such as climbing or detouring around obstacles, can readily propose one, as rationalization does in STaR [32]. These challenges lead to our key insight that failing policy should judge its own repairs. By continuing its flight after each candidate action, the current policy estimates the value of the candidate under its own behavior, which is what approximate policy iteration requires [4850]. This self-verification turns weak sources into reliable supervision. Actions sampled from the policy often contain repair, and rule-based proposals that degrade the policy under direct imitation become its most effective supervision once verified, whereas checking only the next few actions often favors candidates that fail later (Fig. 1(a)). It also reveals how failures evolve. Verified repairs remain valid for subsequent policies, while new failures emerge elsewhere on the same routes (Fig. 1(b)), so supervision must be renewed in every round. Moreover, actions learned from rule-based proposals in one round appear among its sampled actions in the next, indicating that the loop expands what the policy can do rather than reinforcing existing behavior. Based on these insights, we present AERORSI, recursive self-improvement framework that repeats three steps in every round. First, adaptive failure anchoring (AFA) collects the states leading to each failure of the current policy at multiple time scales, so that supervision follows the failures as they are revealed. Starting from these states, continuation-verified repair (CVR) builds candidates from actions sampled from the policy and from rule-based proposals, and accepts candidate only if the original action fails again from the same state or falls clearly behind the best candidate, and the policy completes the candidate again in an independent re-flight. Finally, retentive repair learning (RRL) distills these verified repairs into the policy while keeping its behavior on states that need no repair. Extensive experiments on the TravelUAV benchmark [3] demonstrate the effectiveness of AERORSI. Starting from supervised policy, AERORSI improves the success rate from 46.4% to 67.5% in three rounds and reduces collisions by half (Fig. 1(c)), outperforming the previous stateof-the-art method [1], which is trained from the same policy, by 10.6 points. When built upon the stronger policy of this method, AERORSI further improves the success rate to 69.9%, establishing new state of the art without additional human annotation or inference cost. In summary, our contributions are as follows. We identify three challenges of self-improvement in closed-loop flight and show that letting failing policy judge its own repairs turns its sampled actions and even rule-based proposals into reliable supervision. We reveal that verified repairs remain valid while new failures emerge elsewhere on the routes, and that actions learned from rule-based proposals enter its sampled actions, which together make recursion essential. We propose AERORSI, which anchors the failures of the current policy, verifies candidate repairs by its own continuation, and distills them while keeping its behavior elsewhere, achieving state-of-the-art results on TravelUAV with no extra annotation or inference cost. 2. Related Work We review three lines of work most related to ours, namely aerial vision-language navigation, learning from corrections, and recursive self-improvement. Aerial Vision-Language Navigation. Vision-language navigation was first studied for ground agents [5157] and later extended to UAVs by AerialVLN [2], TravelUAV [3], OpenFly [4], and subsequent benchmarks [57]. Recent methods improve cross-embodiment pretraining [8], longhorizon context modeling [17], robustness to error accumulation [58], future prediction [5963], and spatial reasoning [11, 64, 65]. AerialVLA [9] and AeroDPO [1] show that lightweight vision-language-action policies can match much larger models, and post-training further improves them through preference optimization on synthesized corrections [1] or online reinforcement learning [18, 2931]. These efforts mostly improve the model architecture or learn from synthesized corrections and episode-level rewards, whereas AERORSI learns from repairs that the policy verifies itself, collected anew from its failures in every round, and is complementary to these architectures. Learning from Corrections. Interactive imitation learning asks an expert to label the states that the learner itself encounters, as in DAgger [21] and its variants [2224], while 2 AggreVaTe [66] ranks actions by the cost-to-go of the expert. Navigation policies have also been learned from expert corrections [67] from crashes and disengagements [6870], and in simulation [7173]. To avoid human labeling, recent methods synthesize corrections by collision rollbacks [1], reference paths [27], or auxiliary residual policies [28], and learn from them with supervised, preference, or reinforcement objectives [7477], although preference updates may shift probability to unintended actions [7880]. Since these corrections are judged by an expert, heuristic, reference path, or another policy, none of them accounts for whether the policy itself can execute them. CVR instead judges each candidate by how the current policy, not an expert, continues the flight after it, and RRL imitates the verified best candidate rather than contrasting it with the failed action. Recursive Self-Improvement. Training model on its own verified outputs underlies expert iteration [8183], selftraining [84], STaR [32], and ReST [33, 34], and repeated rounds of it have substantially improved the reasoning of language models [3537, 85], although recent analyses find that it mainly reinforces outputs that the model can already produce [46, 47]. Weak supervisors can still teach stronger models [86], and autocurricula create new challenges as learning proceeds [87]. In robotics and navigation, agents likewise learn from data that they generate themselves [88 90], obtain corrections from residual policies [28], build on coding or multimodal agents [40, 41, 43], direct data collection with learned models [42], or retrain on their own trajectories and reasoning [38, 91, 92], with general formulations in [93, 94]. Closest to ours, CorrectNav [27] repeatedly retrains policy on corrections of its errors toward reference paths, and local recovery supervision [39] checks whether frozen student can continue from teachers recoveries. Rollout-based policy iteration [49, 50] and learning to search [9597] also judge actions by continuation, but roll out every action of small set or follow reference policy. AERORSI brings this judgment to the failures of VLA policy with nearly million actions, verifying candidates from its samples and physical priors by Monte-Carlo continuations from restored states [98100], without reference paths or teacher, and RRL retains its behavior elsewhere, as in continual learning [101103]. Our ablations compare these choices with such combinations (Sec. 4.3): unverified rule-based corrections help little or even hurt, checking only the first actions leaves more collisions, and reusing one round of supervision falls short of anchoring anew in every round. 3. Method section, we first In this formulate recursive selfimprovement for aerial navigation as approximate policy iteration and then present the three modules of AERORSI that implement it in every round. 3.1. Problem Formulation Task. At each step t, the UAV receives an observation ot consisting of its front and downward RGB views and the instruction, together with coarse direction to the target as in the fuzzy direction guidance of [1]. The policy π outputs an action at that discretizes the forward, vertical, and yaw motion, optionally with landing action. An episode succeeds if the UAV lands near the described target, and it terminates at the first failure, namely collision, getting stuck, moving away from the target, landing prematurely, or exceeding the step limit. During training, the simulator can save and restore the full state st of the UAV and its environment and provides depth maps and the target position. AERORSI uses these privileges only to generate training data, and the deployed policy observes ot alone, with the architecture and inference cost of the initial policy π0. Starting from π0, each Recursive Self-Improvement. round generates supervision Dk from the experience of the current policy πk without human annotation and uses Dk to update it to πk+1. From the perspective of approximate policy iteration [48], an ideal round would relabel every state at which πk fails with the improved action a(s) = arg max Qπk (s, a), (1) where Qπk (s, a) is the expected return of executing in and following πk afterward. Because Qπk is defined by the subsequent flight of πk itself, it is the failing policy that should judge its own repairs, as in rollout-based policy iteration [49, 50] and learning to search [95, 96]. Since the judge is the policy itself, each round also improves the next judge, which makes the loop recursive. Two properties of closed-loop flight make this target hard to obtain. The outcome of continuation is stochastic, so single rollout is an unreliable estimate of Qπk . Moreover, as an episode terminates at its first failure, the states that need repair are revealed only as πk improves. AERORSI therefore estimates Qπk from verified continuations of the current policy and relabels the newly revealed failures in every round. 3.2. Overview Fig. 2 illustrates one round of AERORSI. The current policy πk first flies all training routes, and AFA selects anchor states leading to its failures. CVR then turns each anchor into verified repair or discards it, and RRL distills the repairs into πk+1 while keeping the behavior of πk on states that need no repair, and the next round starts from the failures that πk+1 reveals. 3.3. Adaptive Failure Anchoring (AFA) Hand-designed anchors, such as the last action before collision, cover only the failure types and time scales that designer anticipates, whereas the failures of the policy 3 Figure 2. AFA therefore anchors every failure revealed by the current policy at multiple time scales, regardless of its type. For each training episode of πk that ends in failure, AFA places probes at exponentially spaced offsets before the end of the episode. Near offsets capture immediate causes, such as an action into an obstacle, and far offsets capture earlier decisions, such as turn into dead end. Each probe records the saved state s, the observation o, and the action that πk executed. Since the probes far outnumber the anchors that can be verified, AFA draws fixed budget of anchors uniformly from all probes of the round. The anchors therefore follow the failure distribution of πk without hand-crafted rules, so that frequent failure types and time scales receive more anchors, and failures that the policy has overcome receive none. Each anchor is finally assigned an evaluation horizon that grows with its offset and extends beyond the original failure point, so that qualifying candidate must carry the flight past this point. 3.4. Retentive Repair Learning (RRL) policy trained only on repairs tends to drift on states that need no repair, because it transfers the action statistics of the repairs, such as frequent turns, to the rest of the flight. RRL therefore updates the policy with three components that together limit this drift. Repair Supervision. RRL maximizes the likelihood of the verified repair of each anchor and, unlike preference optimization [75], adds no penalty on the original action. The original action is often only moderately worse than the repair and remains correct in many other states, so pushing it down explicitly risks degrading the flight elsewhere. Behavior Retention. Experiments In this section, we first describe the experimental setup and compare AERORSI with existing methods, then ablate its design, and finally present case studies of recorded flights. 4.1. Experimental Setup Benchmark and Metrics. We evaluate AERORSI on TravelUAV [3], benchmark for aerial VLN built on AirSim and 5 Unreal Engine [105]. Its training set contains 7,611 routes in 11 scenes, and its test set contains 1,418 routes in seen environments (Seen), 629 routes with unseen objects (Unseen Object), and 958 routes in unseen environments (Unseen Map). AERORSI collects experience only on the training routes. An episode succeeds if the UAV lands within 20 of the target within 200 actions. Following [1], we report the navigation error (NE, in meters), success rate (SR), oracle success rate (OSR), and success weighted by path length (SPL), together with the collision rate (CR). All design choices were made on training routes held out in preliminary experiments, and every round of AERORSI is evaluated on all test routes. Since closed-loop flight is stochastic, evaluating the same policy twice changes the outcome of about quarter of the routes and its overall SR by up to about two points, so we compare policies route by route and treat smaller differences as noise. The simulator pauses at observation boundaries during data collection so that states can be saved and restored exactly, whereas all evaluations follow the native protocol without pauses. Baselines. We compare with two groups of methods. TravelUAV [3], NavFoM [8], LongFly [17], and NeuroKalman [58] use the L1 assistant guidance of TravelUAV, whereas AerialVLA [9], RefineFly [18], and AeroDPO [1] use fuzzy direction guidance, as AERORSI does. AeroDPO is the closest baseline. It first trains 2B-parameter policy on the expert demonstrations of AerialVLA by supervised fine-tuning, which we denote SFT, and then post-trains it by preference optimization on corrections derived from collision rollbacks. For controlled comparison, AERORSI (SFT init.) starts from the same SFT policy, and we evaluate the released SFT and AeroDPO checkpoints under the same protocol as AERORSI, comparing them route by route. Implementation Details. Table 1 lists the compared policies. To test whether AERORSI also improves policy that has already been post-trained, we further start it from AeroDPO, denoted AERORSI (DPO init.). In both cases, π0 is the initial policy, and the states that need no repair contribute only their observations, labeled with the outputs of the current policy. Sources of Candidates. The two sources of candidates complement each other, and their roles shift as the policy learns (Fig. 4(b, c)). The failing policy often holds repair that it does not choose, as sampled actions supply 44% of the repairs accepted in the first round, and 78% of them still qualify when π0 flies them again, against 38% for new samples that nearly repeat the failed action, so they are not lucky continuations. At the 21% of the anchors whose failure reproduces that only rule-based proposal repaired, however, sampled action of π0 qualifies at only 11%, whereas after one round of learning from both sources, sampled action of π1 qualifies at 62%, as often as at the other anchors, and at 58% of the 42 such anchors in route groups held out from training, against 14% for π0. The repairs learned from the proposals thus enter the policys sampled actions, and the leading source changes across rounds (Fig. 4(c)). The proposals alone lead in the first round, as nearly all of their repairs change single component of the action and thus teach consistent correction, and both sources together lead in the second. No single source suffices in every round, so CVR verifies both and keeps the best candidate. Necessity of Recursion. new round is needed because the failures move, not because the repairs expire (Table 4(b)). Retraining π1 on the repairs of the first round, without anchoring or verifying anew, reaches 60.3%, and collecting twice as many anchors from π0 and training once, with as many updates as two rounds, reaches 63.0%, both below the 66.0% of the second round and with more collisions, whereas the second round without replay still reaches 65.7%. Yet the repairs remain valid, as those verified in the first round still qualify at 87% to 89% of their anchors when 7 Figure 5. Case study of AERORSI. From state before π0 crashes, π0 flies on from each candidate action (top), and π1 flies after one round (bottom). (a) Flying toward the target looks best at first but crashes, whereas turn that falls behind completes the flight, so repair can be judged only by flying on. (b) The sampled actions nearly repeat the crashing action, so only rule-based proposal repairs it, and π1 learns this repair. (c) The same action crashes when π0 flies on but not when π1 does, so every round must judge its repairs anew. later policies continue them, compared with 81% when π0 continues them again (Fig. 4(d)). What changes is where the policy fails. The action at which π0 failed qualifies at 57% to 67% of these anchors under later policies, against 27% under π0, and on the training routes that two consecutive policies both fail, their failure points lie median of 40 apart after the first round and 28 after the second, compared with 13 when the same policy flies twice (Fig. 4(e)). Retentive Repair Learning. Behavior retention keeps the repairs from changing normal flight (Table 4(c)). Training on the repairs alone raises the CR from 29.5% to 32.0%, as the policy turns in 19.6% instead of 15.8% of its actions, drifting toward the 30% of the repairs. Taking the retained states from flights of π0 instead of AeroDPO gives 59.0%, so the retention does not rely on another method. Weighting every qualifying candidate by its group-normalized advantage, as in GRPO [77], is 3.7 points below imitating the best candidate alone, suggesting that one consistent repair per state teaches more than several competing ones. Adding the DPO loss against the original action gives similar 58.0%, while the DPO loss alone collapses the policy, so the gain comes from the verified repairs rather than the objective. Flight Altitude. Many verified repairs climb over obstacles, and the median peak altitude of test flight rises from 10 for π0 to 36 for π3, yet with the altitude capped at 15 above the start on 999 test routes, π3 keeps about four fifths of its gain over π0, 13.2 of 16.2 points (Fig. 4(f)). 4.4. Case Study Missed Repairs. Fig. 5 shows three anchors of the first round, with the front camera in the insets. Panels (a) and (b) reveal two ways in which policy misses repair that exists. In (a), the policy samples the repair but does not choose it. After two actions, sharp turn is about 6 behind the actions flying toward the target, yet those actions crash into palm tree and only the turn completes the flight. repair can thus cost progress before it pays off, so criterion on the first actions would discard exactly the behavior that the policy lacks. In (b), the policy does not even sample the repair, as its sampled actions nearly repeat the action that crashes. Only one of the three rule-based proposals completes the flight, so rules can supply repair, but only the flight of the policy can identify it. In both cases, π1 takes the repair by itself after one round, as do most of its new sampled actions, so each round shifts what the next one can sample. One Action under Two Policies. Fig. 5(c) shows that the value of an action is not fixed. The action at which π0 crashes completes the flight when π1 flies on from it, as it does at most anchors accepted in the first round (Fig. 4(d)). Whether an action repairs failure thus depends on the policy that continues the flight, so label judged under an earlier policy or an expert may not hold for the current one. This is why AERORSI lets the current policy judge its own repairs and verifies them anew in every round. 5. Conclusion In this paper, we have presented AERORSI, recursive self-improvement framework for aerial VLN in which failing policy judges its own repairs by flying on from them. Verified in this way, the sampled actions of the policy and simple rule-based proposals become reliable supervision, and since repairs remain valid while failures move, every round anchors and verifies anew. On TravelUAV, three rounds raise the SR of 2B-parameter policy from 46.4% to 67.5% and reduce collisions by half without additional human labels or changes at deployment.

sections.content: This supplementary material is organized as follows. Sec. gives the implementation details of AERORSI: its settings, the rule-based proposals, the verification of an anchor (Algorithm S1), the ablation variants, and the evaluation and cost. Sec. gives the failure types of both initializations and the paired significance tests behind the comparisons of the main paper. Sec. gives further analyses behind Fig. 4 of the main paper, in the order of its ablation study. A. Implementation Details A.1. Settings Table S1 lists the settings of AERORSI, which are shared by both initializations and all three rounds. fifth of the route groups of the training split is held out from training: the policies still fly these routes and AFA anchors their failures, but their repairs only serve to test whether repairs transfer to route groups that the policy has not learned from (Secs. C.2 and C.3). The retention states of RRL come from successful flights of AeroDPO on the training routes and are labeled with the greedy outputs of the current policy; taking them from the flights of π0 instead gives similar SR (Table 4(c) of the main paper). The proposals are deliberately simple and become useful only after verification (Table 4(a) of the main paper). A.3. Verification Algorithm S1 details how CVR verifies one anchor. flight fails if it collides, lands prematurely, or produces an invalid output, and candidate qualifies if its flight reaches the end of the horizon without failure and with at least 4 of progress, or if it lands successfully. The input check discards an anchor at which the restored observation no longer leads the policy to its original action. The reproduction check keeps an anchor only if the original action is indeed worse than candidate, and the confirmation check accepts candidate only if it qualifies in two independent flights. A.4. Repairs and Failures across Rounds Table S8 flies the 1,048 repairs accepted in the first round again from their anchors, each continued by later policy, as in Fig. 4(d) of the main paper. The repairs remain valid under every later policy, from either source and in the route groups held out from training, whereas the action at which π0 failed passes increasingly often. What changes instead is where the policy fails (Table S9): on the training routes that two consecutive policies both fail, the two failure points lie much farther apart than when one policy flies the same routes twice. Most repairs also hold to the end of the episode. From each of the 1,048 anchors accepted in the first round, π0 executes the verified repair and flies on until it lands, collides, or reaches the limit of 200 actions, with the simulator paused at observation boundaries as in collection. It reaches the target in 57.2% of these episodes, 58.2% for repairs from sampled actions and 56.5% for those from rule-based proposals, and in 53.6% at the 604 anchors whose failure reproduces. The flights that fail again do so median of 14 actions after the original failure point. C.4. Flight Altitude The median peak altitude of test flight of AERORSI (SFT init.) rises from 10.0 in round 0 to 15.6, 29.1, and 36.2 in rounds 1 to 3. To test how much of the gain this explains, we evaluate π0, π1, and π3 on 999 test routes drawn from the three splits with the altitude capped at 15 above the start of each route, cutting any upward command to the room left below the cap. With the cap, their SR is 36.44%, 45.25%, and 49.65%, against 50.15%, 58.36%, and 66.37% without it on the same routes, so π3 keeps 13.21 of its 16.22point gain over π0 (Fig. 4(f) of the main paper).
